Enhanced fan-out can be used only with KCL 2.0 and above, and these apps are already on that version, so they can switch by changing only the library's retrieval setting without code changes. The stream is in a single AWS account and all five consumers run in the same Region. Which improvement is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Double the number of shards to increase the total shared read throughput across shards.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Have each consumer call GetRecords more often by shortening the polling interval and increase the number of calling threads to match the number of consumers to reduce delay.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Register the consumers as enhanced fan-out consumers so that each consumer receives dedicated read throughput per shard.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Extend the stream retention period to 7 days so that data is not lost even if consumers fall behind.

explanation: Shared throughput consumers split 2 MB/s of reads per shard, so propagation delay grows as consumers increase, and enhanced fan-out is supported with KCL 2.0 and above (if an app is KCL 1.x, the version must be upgraded first), and because these apps are already on that version, they can use it just by switching a setting. Enhanced fan-out gives each registered consumer dedicated read throughput per shard and pushes records, so the contention disappears. Adding shards violates the constraint that write costs increase and also leaves the shared structure among consumers unchanged. Increasing polling runs into the per-shard read call limit and shared throughput even faster and does not resolve the contention. Extending retention only prevents data loss, does not reduce delay, and increases storage cost. Because the company must avoid adding shards that increase write cost and eliminate contention between consumers, an approach that gives each consumer dedicated throughput is right.

prompt: A media company wants on-premises servers to access Amazon S3 over a private path through AWS Direct Connect without traversing the internet. Under security policy, on premises must access S3 only through private IP addresses inside a VPC, not S3 public IPs, and a public virtual interface and allowing the S3 public IP ranges are not permitted. Workloads inside the VPC in the same Region should access S3 at no additional cost. On-premises servers look up S3 names through the internal DNS, and the network team also wants to reduce NAT gateway usage cost. This configuration applies to one VPC in the Seoul Region. On premises already has a private virtual interface configured over Direct Connect and has internal DNS servers. S3 access targets only buckets in the Seoul Region, and the network team can set up DNS conditional forwarding. When EC2 workloads in the same VPC access S3, no additional hourly charge should be incurred. The security team must prove at audit time that traffic from on premises to S3 was never placed on an internet route table under any circumstances. There is only one S3 bucket Region, Seoul. DNS lookups from both on premises and the VPC must go to the correct endpoint. Which actions must be taken to configure this to meet both requirements? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create only an S3 gateway endpoint, and route the on-premises routes advertised over Direct Connect toward the gateway endpoint.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create an S3 interface VPC endpoint so that on premises can access S3 with private IP addresses.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Add a static route toward the S3 public IP ranges on the on-premises servers and communicate through a public virtual interface.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Apply the interface endpoint's private DNS only to the inbound Resolver endpoint, and have workloads inside the VPC use the gateway endpoint.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Send on-premises traffic out to the S3 public endpoint through the NAT gateway in a private subnet.

explanation: A gateway endpoint cannot be used for traffic from on premises, from peered VPCs in other Regions, or through a transit gateway, so an interface endpoint is needed for on-premises private IP access. In that case, if private DNS is applied only to the inbound Resolver endpoint, on-premises lookups go to the interface endpoint's private IP and in-VPC lookups go to the gateway endpoint, so the interface endpoint charges are incurred only for on-premises traffic. A gateway endpoint alone cannot be reached from on premises. A NAT gateway is for workloads inside the VPC, is not a path for on-premises traffic, and also incurs data processing charges. A public VIF and a public IP path violate the security policy that access must be only through private IPs. Because on premises must use only private IPs and VPC workloads must incur no additional cost, the two kinds of endpoints are used separately by purpose.

prompt: A security operations team wants to receive high-severity GuardDuty findings and Config noncompliance events from 80 organization accounts in a central security account and run an automated isolation Lambda function. Accounts are added frequently, and the central account's credentials or long-term access keys must not be stored in each account. The event forwarding rules and the forwarding IAM roles in each account are already set up to be deployed automatically to new accounts by the account baseline StackSet. The security team does not want to ask each account owner for separate configuration even as accounts grow, and the delay from when an event occurs until the isolation Lambda function runs must be within 1 minute. The isolation Lambda function runs in the central account, and the permission to isolate target accounts is already configured through role delegation. The event types are GuardDuty findings and Config compliance changes, and thousands occur per day. The central security account has 3 owners and does not want to manage separate queues or subscriptions for each account. The IAM role for event forwarding is already deployed in each account, and the central account's event bus name is the same in every account. The target events are small and do not hit forwarding limits. Which configuration meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Put a resource policy on the central account event bus that allows PutEvents from organization accounts with the aws:PrincipalOrgID condition, have each account's rule specify the central bus as its target, and have a central rule invoke the Lambda function.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Publish events from each account to an Amazon SNS topic, and have a Lambda function in the central account subscribe to all topics with IAM user access keys.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Send each account's events to Amazon CloudWatch Logs, and have a Lambda function in the central account query the log groups of all accounts every 5 minutes to check the conditions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Create a separate event bus per account ID in the central account, and operate a procedure that adds the new account's ID to the bus policy whenever a new account is created.

explanation: The resource-based policy of an EventBridge event bus can grant permission with an organization condition, so new accounts can send events without modifying the central policy, and because the rule deployed as part of the baseline specifies the central bus as its target, no long-term credentials are needed. The SNS subscription and access key approach violates the constraint of not storing long-term keys. Log polling has a 5-minute interval, so it cannot meet the 1-minute isolation requirement, and it requires giving query permissions to all accounts, which is a heavy operational burden. Per-account-ID buses and the policy modification procedure require human intervention for every new account, so they do not suit an environment where accounts are added frequently. The conditions of no long-term credentials and no configuration needed even as accounts grow point to a central event bus with an organization-level resource policy.

prompt: A company must deploy an audit IAM role and a CloudWatch alarm baseline to 120 accounts in 3 organizational units (OUs) in its organization and to accounts created in the future. The baseline template is revised once or twice a month, and revisions must be applied consistently to all accounts. The company does not want to create a pre-provisioned administrator role in each account. Deployment results must be viewable in one place, and when a new account is created, the baseline must be in place within a day. The security team wants to minimize the principals that have permission to deploy IAM roles. The baseline contains one IAM role that auditors use read-only and 12 CloudWatch alarms, and the names must be identical in all accounts. New accounts are created by Control Tower, and the target OUs do not change. The security team wants to see on one screen which account failed and why when a deployment fails. Currently, every time an account is created, the owner manually copies the baseline in the console, which often causes omissions lasting weeks, and an audit finding noted that some accounts remain on an older version after revisions. The baseline targets only the Seoul Region, not all Regions. Which method meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Use a self-managed StackSet, manually create a StackSet execution role in each account, and directly specify and update the list of target accounts for deployment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Share an AWS Service Catalog portfolio with the organization and ask each account administrator to launch the baseline product themselves.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create a service-managed AWS CloudFormation StackSet for the target OUs with trusted access enabled with AWS Organizations, and enable automatic deployment so that template revisions and deployment to new accounts are handled automatically.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Have a script in the management account assume the OrganizationAccountAccessRole and deploy the stack to each account in a loop, detect new accounts with a weekly cron job and deploy to them, and have an owner retry failed accounts manually.

explanation: A service-managed StackSet automatically configures the required roles through Organizations trusted access, so no per-account pre-provisioned role is needed. With automatic deployment on, the stack is deployed automatically to accounts added to the target OUs, and updating the template applies the same change to all target accounts. The self-managed method conflicts with the constraint of having to create an execution role in each account. Service Catalog requires account administrators to launch it themselves, so it does not result in consistent enforced deployment. A looping script and cron are self-built automation, so you are responsible for error handling and revision consistency yourself, and reflecting new accounts is delayed by up to a week. Because the baseline must be deployed automatically, even to new accounts, without a pre-provisioned administrator role, a service-managed StackSet is right.

prompt: A financial group operates 140 member accounts in AWS Organizations across multiple OUs, and new accounts are created every week. Because of data residency regulations, it must preventively block resource creation in Regions other than Seoul (ap-northeast-2) and N. Virginia (us-east-1), and the actions of the account root user are also in scope. However, calls to global services such as IAM, Amazon CloudFront, and Amazon Route 53 must continue to work. The security team manages policy change history in a code repository, and this control must be deployed before the external audit next quarter. Besides the approved Regions, some services provide global endpoints only in us-east-1. The team wants a staged rollout in which the policy is applied first to a test OU to check the impact and then broadened to the root. Policy documents go through code review in Git, the security team has 3 people, and no exception accounts are allowed. The service-linked roles and the management account are outside the effect of SCPs, so it has already been decided to put a separate control on the management account side. This question targets all principals in member accounts, including the root user. Which method that applies automatically to new accounts without per-account manual work has the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Leave the default FullAWSAccess SCP as is, and additionally attach to the root an SCP with an Allow statement that permits only the approved Regions so that actions in other Regions are blocked, opening the global services with a separate Allow statement.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deploy AWS Config rules to all accounts to detect resources created in nonapproved Regions, and configure a Lambda function to delete those resources immediately upon detection.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Attach to the IAM users and roles in each member account a permissions boundary that denies actions in nonapproved Regions, and have the account creation pipeline apply the same permissions boundary automatically.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Attach to the organization root an SCP that denies when aws:RequestedRegion is not an approved Region, and exclude global service actions from the deny with NotAction.

explanation: A Deny SCP attached to the organization root is inherited by all child OUs and new accounts and also applies to the account root user, so using the aws:RequestedRegion condition together with a NotAction exception for global services implements the preventive control in one step. An SCP that adds an Allow statement while FullAWSAccess is kept blocks nothing, because a policy allowing all actions remains. The AWS Config and Lambda deletion approach reacts after the resource is created, so it is after-the-fact detection and does not meet the preventive requirement. A permissions boundary applies only to IAM users and roles, so it cannot block the root user and needs application work in every account. Note, however, that SCPs do not apply to the management account. Because the control must also block the root user and make global services exceptions, an aws:RequestedRegion deny SCP with a NotAction exception is right.

prompt: A SaaS company connects production (prod) VPCs in 6 accounts, development (dev) VPCs in 9 accounts, and a shared services VPC that hosts common tools to a single transit gateway. Communication between production and development VPCs must be blocked at the network level, both environments must be able to reach the shared services VPC, and adding a new VPC must not require modifying the existing routing configuration. The network team has only 3 people and cannot handle routing change requests manually, and during compliance reviews the isolation between environments must be demonstrated through the routing configuration. Isolation between environments is verified through routing, and 2 to 3 new VPCs are created each month. The shared services VPC hosts DNS, CI tools, and an artifact repository, which both environments must reach. The CIDRs of all VPCs do not overlap, and the transit gateway is in a single Region, Seoul. The servers in the shared services VPC must respond to requests from both environments, so the return path must also work in both directions. Isolating with network ACLs or security groups alone is not accepted by auditors. Which design meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create separate transit gateway route tables for production, development, and shared services, associate each attachment with its corresponding table, propagate only the shared services route to the production and development tables, and propagate the routes of both environments to the shared services table.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Propagate the routes of all attachments to a single default route table, and set deny rules for the other environment's CIDR in the security groups and network ACLs of the production and development VPCs.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Enter blackhole static routes in the default route table that point production and development CIDRs at each other, and update the blackhole routes with the new CIDR every time a VPC is added.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Create separate transit gateways per environment and connect each to the shared services VPC with VPC peering, create no peering between production and development, allocate separate CIDR ranges to each environment, and have each environment's team approve routing changes.

explanation: If you associate attachments with per-environment transit gateway route tables and propagate only the required routes, production and development do not have each other's routes, so they are separated at the network level, and a new VPC only needs to be associated with the corresponding table and propagated to the shared services table. Blocking with security groups and ACLs on a single default table leaves routing open, so it is not network-level separation, and the rules grow with every account. Blackhole static routes require editing CIDRs every time a VPC is added, which violates the requirement not to modify the existing configuration. Mixing per-environment transit gateways with peering increases the number of gateways and peering connections and adds more operational burden. Because routing changes must not be needed when VPCs are added and isolation must be demonstrated through routing, separating TGW route tables and using propagation is right.

prompt: A retailer's network team controls VPCs, subnets, route tables, and NAT gateways in a central network account, and wants the 30 application team accounts in the same organization to deploy Amazon EC2 and Amazon RDS directly into that network. Teams must not be able to see each other's resources and must not be able to change routing or subnet configuration, and the goal is to reduce the number of VPCs to manage and the cost of connections between accounts (peering and transit gateway attachments). The security team must demonstrate at audit time that team accounts cannot arbitrarily change subnets and routing, and the network team wants to consolidate NAT gateway costs in one place. Application teams must be able to launch their own EC2 and RDS directly in the subnets, but security groups are managed by the team accounts themselves. The central network account operates the NAT gateways and VPC flow logs in one place, and all 30 accounts are in the same organization and the same Region. RDS is owned by the team accounts, and the central account is not involved in subnet group configuration. Isolation between teams has already been agreed upon through security groups and IAM. The network team has 3 people. Which approach MOST appropriately meets the requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create a VPC in each team account and connect them all to a transit gateway, control traffic with the central route table, and give teams no permission to modify attachments.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create a VPC in each team account, establish VPC peering with the network VPC, and restrict permission to edit route tables with IAM policies so that teams cannot change routes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Have the network account share the subnets with the team accounts in the organization by using AWS RAM, and have the team accounts deploy their own resources directly into the shared subnets.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Publish the service in the network VPC as a PrivateLink endpoint service, and have each team account VPC create an interface endpoint to access it.

explanation: With VPC subnet sharing, the VPC owner (the network account) shares subnets with participant accounts in the same organization, and the participant accounts create their own resources such as EC2 and RDS in those subnets, cannot see other participants' resources, and the number of VPCs and cross-account connections also decreases. Routing and subnets are controlled by the owner. Creating a VPC per team and joining them with a transit gateway increases VPCs and attachments in proportion to the number of accounts, which is the opposite of the reduction goal. VPC peering also increases VPCs and connections per account and weakens control because teams own their own VPCs. PrivateLink is a service-level access mechanism and not a way to deploy team resources into a central network. Because teams must not be able to change subnet configuration and the number of VPCs and NAT cost must be reduced, RAM subnet sharing is right.

prompt: A fintech's payment lookup API runs hundreds of AWS Lambda functions concurrently and connects to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL. During every marketing event, the number of connections reaches max_connections, causing connection errors and CPU spikes. Requests should be queued and processed rather than rejected whenever possible, and application changes must be limited to replacing the connection endpoint. The database is already a Multi-AZ configuration, the write load is not high, and a secondary goal is to reduce the time application connections are dropped during a failover. The Lambda functions are written in Node.js, and concurrency rises to 10 times normal during events. The connection information is specified by a host name in an environment variable, so only the endpoint string needs to be changed, and with a team of 3, there is no capacity to write and maintain connection pooling logic ourselves. Events are held two or three times per quarter. A recent incident report recorded that when payment lookup requests are rejected during connection errors, retries from merchant apps flood in and make the situation worse. Which improvement is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lower the Lambda function reserved concurrency to at or below the database max_connections to throttle excess requests, and modify the client code so that callers retry with exponential backoff.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Scale the Aurora instance to a larger class to raise the max_connections value and leave function concurrency as it is.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Change the Lambda code to open a new connection on each invocation and close it immediately after processing so that idle connections do not accumulate.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Place Amazon RDS Proxy in front of the Aurora cluster and have the Lambda functions connect to the proxy endpoint so that database connections are pooled and reused.

explanation: RDS Proxy maintains and reuses a connection pool and queues or throttles connections that cannot be handled immediately, so spiking Lambda connections do not overwhelm the database, and it can be introduced just by replacing the endpoint. Lowering with reserved concurrency throttles excess requests, which conflicts with the requirement not to reject requests. Scaling up the instance raises the limit but leaves the connection surge pattern unchanged, so it only adds cost and does not solve the root cause. Opening and closing a connection on each invocation increases connection creation load and actually worsens the problem. Application changes must be limited to replacing the endpoint and requests should be queued whenever possible, so a connection pooling proxy is right, while throttling rejects requests.

prompt: A company that is migrating from Oracle to Aurora PostgreSQL using a DMS full load and CDC is preparing for cutover. It wants to switch over with no data loss or inconsistency at cutover. The source database operates until just before the switch, and downtime must be short. The source Oracle receives writes until just before the switch, and the migration team performed one rehearsal before cutover. Some of the target tables have LOB columns, so it is hard to be confident of consistency from row counts alone. The Oracle source retains archive logs for the last 3 days, and the DMS replication instance has ample CPU headroom. Cutover approval is given by two owners only after they review evidence of data consistency, and the evidence must include validation results provided by DMS. The cutover window is 2 hours starting at 2 AM. Some tables in the source Oracle have no primary key, which made change tracking tricky, and in the rehearsal the row counts of two tables temporarily diverged and were resolved as CDC caught up. After the switch, the source is kept read-only for a week. Which two actions meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: In the cutover window, stop application writes, confirm that the DMS source and target CDC latency metrics are close to 0 and that validation has passed, and then switch the connections to the target database.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Before cutover, reduce the source database's change log retention period to the minimum so that DMS has less log to read and CDC runs faster. Record the rehearsal results on the team wiki and check the change log retention period again.

choices.label: C
choices.text: While the source is still receiving writes, stop the DMS task immediately and switch connections to the target database, and clean up changes after the stop with a later batch.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Just before starting the cutover, restart the DMS task with the reload-target option to reload the tables from scratch, which automatically guarantees consistency.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Turn on DMS data validation to compare row-level consistency between the source and the target, and resolve the cause for tables where mismatches are reported before cutover.

explanation: The correct answers are data validation and confirming that CDC lag has cleared after stopping writes. Validation finds data mismatches between the source and the target, and if you confirm that CDC lag has disappeared after stopping writes, you can switch over with the last change reflected on the target. CDC has no real-time guarantee and lag can grow to several minutes or more, so confirmation is necessary. reload-target reloads from scratch, which increases downtime and risk and does not automatically guarantee consistency. Stopping the task right away on a source that is still being written to loses changes. Reducing log retention may prevent DMS from reading the logs it needs. Because loss and inconsistency at the switch must be prevented and LOB columns make row counts alone insufficient, both confirming lag clearance after stopping writes and data validation are needed.

prompt: A fintech company runs its payment ledger on an Amazon Aurora MySQL cluster in us-east-1. Regulations require that, in the event of a complete Regional failure, writes be resumed in another Region within a few minutes and that data loss be within a few seconds. In addition, the analytics team in ap-northeast-2 must be able to query the same data read-only from a nearby Region during normal operation. The current DR copies snapshots to another Region and takes tens of minutes to recover. The application already uses an Aurora MySQL 8.0-compatible version, so replacing the engine or large-scale code changes is difficult, and management requires Region failover drills every quarter. The ledger data is currently about 3 TB and is expected to triple over the next 2 years. Analytics queries run several times a day and must not affect the write cluster. Region failover drills are held quarterly, pausing writes briefly during a drill is acceptable, and the infrastructure is managed with AWS CloudFormation. Management required recovery to a state where writes are possible during a Regional failure, not a read-only state, and the snapshot restore method took 40 minutes in a drill, exceeding the criterion. The application connections are specified only by the cluster endpoint name. Which configuration meets the above requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Schedule cross-Region copies with AWS Backup every 5 minutes, and during a failure restore a new Aurora cluster in ap-northeast-2 from the most recent recovery point and change the connection information. In every drill, create a new cluster with the same procedure and verify normal operation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create a separate Aurora MySQL cluster in ap-northeast-2 and synchronize it with an AWS DMS ongoing replication (CDC) task, and during a failure stop the replication task and switch the application over.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Add a secondary cluster in ap-northeast-2 with an Aurora global database to handle analytics reads during normal operation, and during a Regional failure promote (fail over) the secondary cluster to the new primary cluster.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Distribute the Aurora replicas of the us-east-1 cluster across three Availability Zones to prepare for Availability Zone failures, and keep the existing snapshot copy procedure for Regional failures.

explanation: The correct answer is an Aurora global database. It replicates to the secondary Region with dedicated storage-layer infrastructure, usually with latency of under 1 second, so the RPO is a few seconds, promoting the secondary cluster resumes writes within a few minutes, and during normal operation readers in the secondary Region also handle read queries. Restoring a new cluster from a recovery point has a long restore time like the snapshot approach, so it cannot meet an RTO of a few minutes. DMS CDC has no SLA on replication lag, which can grow to several minutes or more, and the replication task and the switchover procedure must be operated by you. A configuration that only spreads Availability Zones within the same Region does not protect against a complete Regional failure. The requirements of an RTO of a few minutes, an RPO of a few seconds, and nearby reads during normal operation are met by a single global database secondary cluster.

prompt: A financial affiliate is building a dedicated network connecting two on-premises data centers to AWS. The target availability SLA for the critical workloads is 99.99%, and connectivity must be maintained even if an entire single AWS Direct Connect location goes down. The company wants to meet this requirement, which goes beyond the development and test level, without ordering more connections than necessary. The two data centers are near Seoul and each requires 10 Gbps or more of bandwidth. The network team wants to order with the connection wizard of the Resiliency Toolkit and to spend on monthly port costs only at the necessary level. The two data centers each have separate ISP circuits and are currently connected only through an internet VPN. The budget owner wants to use only as many locations and ports as needed, but the 99.99% SLA requirement is an audit item and cannot be compromised. Port speed is standardized at 10 Gbps. Traffic from each data center to AWS averages 3 Gbps per day, and an incident in which an entire location went down occurred once in the past. The network team has 4 people and will configure the Direct Connect gateway and virtual interfaces themselves after the wizard. Which configuration is MOST appropriate based on the Direct Connect Resiliency Toolkit?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Order two dedicated connections that terminate on different devices at a single Direct Connect location, create a virtual interface on each of the two connections, and make them redundant with BGP.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A Maximum resiliency model in which you order two dedicated connections at each of two or more different Direct Connect locations, with each connection terminating on a different Direct Connect device.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A High resiliency model that orders only one dedicated connection at each of two different locations, terminating on one device per location, and uses both connections as active. Order one 10 Gbps connection per location to lower port cost.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Place one dedicated connection at a single location and configure an internet-based Site-to-Site VPN as a backup path that reroutes BGP routes through the VPN when the dedicated connection fails.

explanation: The correct answer is the Maximum resiliency model. Placing connections at two or more locations and terminating each on separate devices tolerates device, connection, and entire location failures and targets the 99.99% SLA. A configuration that only splits devices within one location is the development and test model and is vulnerable to a location failure. The High resiliency model with one connection per location has a target SLA of 99.9%, which falls short of the requirement. A single connection with a VPN backup can survive a location failure but does not satisfy the 99.99% dedicated connection SLA requirement. The requirements of an entire single location failure and a 99.99% SLA point to the Maximum resiliency model with dual connections at different locations.

prompt: A securities firm's Java Lambda API receives a rush of requests just before market open between 08:50 and 09:30 on weekdays, and traffic is low at other times. During this period, cold starts cause p99 latency to exceed the SLA. Keeping provisioned concurrency all day would be too costly, and the traffic pattern is the same every day. The function uses Java 17 and takes 3 seconds to initialize, 20 times the usual requests arrive during the 30 minutes just before market open, and latency during the rest of the day is within the SLA. The function is already deployed with published versions and an alias, and the alias is connected to API Gateway. It is enough for capacity to be ready 30 minutes before market open, and there is no market open on weekday holidays. SnapStart is not considered in this scope, and the team has 3 people. The operations team wants to make configuration changes without a code deployment. During the 30 minutes before market open, responses must be within target even when 20 times the usual requests arrive, and after market open, traffic quickly returns to the usual level. The company wants to leave the function memory and code as they are and adjust only the settings. Which method meets the SLA MOST cost-effectively?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Set provisioned concurrency on the function's $LATEST version at the market-open peak level and keep it all day.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create an alias for a published version of the function and set provisioned concurrency on it, and use Application Auto Scaling scheduled actions to increase it just before market open and decrease it afterward.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Set the function's reserved concurrency to the peak level so that execution environments are initialized in advance before market open.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Raise the function memory to the maximum and warm up the execution environments with an Amazon EventBridge rule that invokes the function at 5-minute intervals before market open, starting the invocations 30 minutes before open and continuing after open.

explanation: Provisioned concurrency secures pre-initialized execution environments and eliminates cold starts, and it can be configured only on a version or an alias. If the pattern is predictable, Application Auto Scaling scheduled scaling can raise it only during peak hours to reduce cost. Provisioned concurrency cannot be set on $LATEST, and keeping it all day also violates the cost constraint. Reserved concurrency only secures capacity and does not pre-initialize environments, so it does not solve cold starts. Warming with periodic invocations does not guarantee as many concurrent environments as are needed at the same time, and increasing memory only raises cost. Because capacity is needed only for the 30 minutes just before market open and the pattern is the same every day, increase and decrease the provisioned concurrency of the published version with scheduled scaling.

prompt: A payments platform team wants consuming accounts' VPCs (40 accounts in the organization) to call an authentication API that runs in a private subnet in account A. The CIDRs of the consumer VPCs overlap with each other, and some are the same 10.0.0.0/16 as the provider VPC, and CIDR reassignment is not possible. The entire provider network must not be exposed to the consumer side, and only one-way access, in which the consumer accounts initiate calls to the provider, is needed. The consumer account teams have different schedules and cannot negotiate CIDRs with the provider, and the provider team does not want to change its own network configuration, such as routing, peering, and CIDRs, as consumer accounts are added (registering allowed principals on the endpoint service is fine). There are 40 consumer accounts in total, and 1 to 2 are added every week. The authentication API is served over TLS behind an NLB, and the call volume is thousands of requests per second. Some consumer VPCs have the same CIDR as the provider VPC, so peering or a TGW connection cannot be established at all. The security team wants only consumer accounts allowed by the provider to have access. The API terminates TLS at the NLB, and requests arrive only on TCP 443. Each account team manages the consumer VPC's routing configuration directly, and the central network team is not involved. Which configuration MOST appropriately meets the requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Connect account A and all 40 consumer VPCs to a transit gateway, and configure the TGW route tables so that only the API subnet route is propagated.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Connect the VPC in account A to each consumer VPC with VPC peering, and allow only traffic to the API port in the consumer-side security groups.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Connect each consumer VPC to a virtual private gateway in account A with a Site-to-Site VPN, restrict the exposed subnets to the API subnet with a routing policy, and narrow the access scope once more with consumer-side security groups.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Put an NLB in front of the API in account A and publish it as a VPC endpoint service, register the root ARNs of the 40 consumer accounts as allowed principals, and have each consumer VPC access it through an interface VPC endpoint.

explanation: With PrivateLink, an endpoint network interface is created in a subnet of the consumer VPC, the service is accessed through a consumer-side private IP, the connection is initiated by the consumer, and only the endpoint service (behind the NLB) is exposed rather than the entire provider network, so it works even when CIDRs overlap. If you register only consumer account ARNs as allowed principals, only the allowed accounts can create endpoints. VPC peering cannot be created between VPCs with overlapping CIDRs and does not support transitive routing. A transit gateway cannot route VPC attachments with overlapping CIDRs together in one route table, so it has the same problem. A VPN causes route conflicts when the CIDRs on both sides overlap, requires operating a tunnel for each VPC, and limiting exposure at the subnet level is also incomplete. Because the CIDRs overlap, only one-way access is needed, and no network changes are allowed on the provider side, PrivateLink is the only one that works.

prompt: A company is replicating 30 order system servers with AWS Application Migration Service (MGN) and has a cutover window of 2 hours starting at 2 AM at the end of the month. All replication is healthy, and the application team wants to minimize cutover risk. A cutover instance does not receive changes from the source server after it is launched. It must be possible to return to the source server if a problem occurs. The 30 servers are divided into web, application, and database tiers, and write transactions keep arriving at the database. If service normalization is not confirmed by 4 AM, when the window ends, the company must fall back to the source servers. The 30 servers consist of 12 web, 12 application, and 6 database servers. A post-launch configuration script must run on each replicated server, and test instances can be launched several times outside the cutover window. The criterion for the rollback decision is whether the core business flows are normal by 4 AM. After cutover, the database tier receives writes on the new instances, so changes after cutover are not reflected on the source. Considering this, the scope of data loss at the time of rollback must be explained to management in advance, and DNS must also be switched back when returning. Which cutover plan is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Without any separate testing, launch the cutover instances as soon as the window opens, and keep the source servers accepting writes during cutover with replication maintained so that changes automatically follow to AWS. Before cutover, match the target instance security groups to the source's and keep the source running.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Immediately after launching the cutover instances, click finalize cutover right away to clean up the replication resources, and if a problem occurs, recover by re-creating new instances instead of using the source servers.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Launch the cutover instances one hour before the cutover window opens, keep the source servers in service until the window closes, and then switch over by changing only DNS.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Verify functionality with test instances before cutover; when the window opens, stop application writes, confirm that replication has caught up, launch the cutover instances and validate them, and finalize the cutover only after stability is confirmed.

explanation: The correct answer is pre-testing, stopping writes and confirming replication sync, launching and validating the cutover instances, and finalizing after stability is confirmed. A cutover instance reflects the latest state at launch time and does not receive later source changes, so writes must be stopped first to prevent data loss. Finalizing the cutover stops replication, cleans up replicated data and resources, and removes the agent, which eliminates any room for rollback, so it must be done after validation. If you let the source keep receiving writes, the changes are not reflected on the cutover instances and the data diverges. An instance launched in advance also does not receive changes after that point. Because changes are not reflected on the source after cutover and because of the rollback deadline, pre-testing and stopping writes are needed, and finalization must come after stability is confirmed.

prompt: An insurance company operates 25 VPCs (in 12 accounts) connected with a transit gateway in the Seoul Region and connected to an on-premises data center with AWS Direct Connect. On-premises servers need to resolve the name (app.internal.example) in an AWS private hosted zone, and all AWS VPCs need to resolve the on-premises domain corp.example.com. The network team decided not to add staff for DNS server patching and incident response, and name resolution must not be interrupted by the failure of a single Availability Zone. The on-premises DNS servers can forward queries over Direct Connect to private IP addresses in AWS, and conversely, queries for the on-premises domain are answered by two on-premises DNS servers. The VPC private hosted zone is associated with the shared services VPC and with each VPC. Query volume is thousands per second. Long latency in on-premises domain resolution leads to login failures, so the forwarding path must be redundant across Availability Zones. The network team wants to configure the endpoints only once and handle growth in accounts just by sharing rules. Which configuration is the MOST cost-effective, without operating EC2 for DNS forwarders yourself and without creating duplicate endpoints per account?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create Amazon Route 53 Resolver inbound and outbound endpoints in the shared services VPC that use IP addresses in two or more Availability Zones, share the corp.example.com forwarding rule with the organization through AWS RAM and associate it with each VPC, and associate the private hosted zone with the shared services VPC as well.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Configure two DNS forwarder EC2 instances in the shared services VPC with two-way conditional forwarding, point the DHCP option sets of all VPCs at these servers, and have the network team handle server OS patching and incident response.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create outbound endpoints and forwarding rules separately for every VPC in each account, register all the VPC inbound endpoint IPs in the on-premises DNS, and update this registration every time a VPC is added.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Replicate the on-premises domain into a Route 53 public hosted zone so that VPCs resolve it over the internet path, publish the private zone records publicly so that on premises can query them, and rely on internet DNS for internal name resolution.

explanation: If you place an inbound endpoint in the shared services VPC, on premises can query the private hosted zone associated with that VPC, and if you share the outbound endpoint and forwarding rule through RAM and associate them with each VPC, all VPCs forward corp.example.com to on premises without creating duplicate endpoints in each account. Forwarder EC2 instances conflict with the constraint that you would have to operate them yourself. Creating endpoints per VPC violates the prohibition on duplicate creation and is less cost-efficient because hourly endpoint charges increase. Replicating into a public hosted zone exposes internal names externally, which is a security problem, and it is also not a private name resolution architecture. Because the company must avoid operating EC2 forwarders and avoid creating duplicate endpoints in each account, the shared services VPC Resolver endpoints with RAM rule sharing are right.

prompt: A manufacturing company charges back the costs of 60 accounts in AWS Organizations to departments based on the CostCenter tag. Teams use the tag keys costcenter, CostCenter, and cost-center inconsistently and with different value formats, so Cost Explorer aggregation is off. The finance team wants to standardize key spelling and allowed values at the organization level, prevent noncompliant tagging, and view costs classified by a single standard key. The chargeback report closes at the beginning of each month, so the standard must be applied within this month, and the manual work of the report author converting tag values separately must be eliminated. The tags are currently used across Amazon EC2 instances and Amazon S3 buckets, and both are resource types supported by enforced_for in tag policies. The standard key is decided as CostCenter alone, and the allowed values are a list created by the finance team (40 department codes). The company wants new resources with incorrect tags to be blocked at creation time, and cleanup of already created resources will be a separate later task. The chargeback report is created by grouping by the CostCenter tag in Cost Explorer, and the finance team updates the department code list quarterly. The policy must be applied within this month, so approaches that require code changes or development deployments are difficult. Which combination MOST appropriately meets these requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In the billing console of each member account, activate all three tag keys as cost allocation tags, create a report per key in Cost Explorer, and add up the numbers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Use an AWS Config required-tags rule to detect resources without tags and send a weekly report, delegate key spelling cleanup to each team lead to do manually every quarter, and have the finance team check compliance through the report.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Use AWS Cost Categories rules to map the values of the three keys to departments for reporting, and let teams keep using the tag keys they use now.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Define the CostCenter key spelling and allowed values in an Organizations tag policy, specify enforced_for for ec2:instance and s3:bucket to block noncompliant tagging at creation time, and activate CostCenter as a cost allocation tag in the billing console of the management account.

explanation: A tag policy defines the capitalization of tag keys and allowed values at the organization level, and for resource types specified with enforced_for (ec2:instance and s3:bucket support enforcement, whereas for example RDS DB instances support report-only mode and not enforcement), noncompliant tagging can be blocked at creation time. The standardized CostCenter key must be activated as a cost allocation tag in the management account for it to appear in Cost Explorer and reports. Activating it in member accounts does not work because the management account is the only place in an organization that can access the cost allocation tags manager. A Config rule only reports missing tags after the fact and cannot standardize spelling or block. Cost Categories are for classification in reports, do not block noncompliant tagging, and leave the sprawl of tag keys in place. Because the standard must be applied within this month and the report author's manual work must be eliminated, tag policies together with activating the cost allocation tag are right.

prompt: An advertising analytics team loads hundreds of GB of CSV logs per day into Amazon S3 and queries them with Amazon Athena. Most queries look up only specific campaign IDs from the last 3 days, but every query scans the entire table, so the monthly Athena bill is large and queries are slow. The analysts' SQL must be preserved, and the team does not want to operate a new cluster. Analysts use standard SQL, and a BI tool connects through the Athena JDBC driver. The goal is to cut query cost by half or more within this quarter. The CSV files are already stored in S3 under date-based prefixes, there are about 60 columns, and queries reference fewer than ten of them. One nightly transformation run is sufficient, and new data is transformed and accumulated the same way. The team has 2 people and wants to avoid services that must be operated around the clock. The original CSV files are kept for archival purposes. Query results refresh the BI dashboard every morning, and analysts must be able to query by the same table name without changing their SQL. Data older than the last 3 days is rarely queried but must be retained for 1 year for auditing. Which improvement is the MOST cost-effective?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Change the S3 bucket storage class to Intelligent-Tiering to lower the storage unit price of the data that queries scan, and adjust lifecycle rules together.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Convert the data to Parquet with AWS Glue ETL or Athena CTAS and partition it by date so that queries read only the needed partitions and columns.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create an Amazon Redshift provisioned cluster, load the CSV files, and have analysts query with Redshift.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Turn off Athena query result reuse and increase the number of concurrent queries to shorten processing time.

explanation: Athena is billed by the amount of data scanned, so converting to a columnar format (Parquet) reads only the needed columns, and adding date partitions scans only the partitions of the last 3 days, which reduces both cost and time, while the same SQL keeps working and the serverless model is maintained. The storage class concerns the storage unit price and does not change Athena's scan-based billing. A Redshift cluster brings new operational burden and violates the constraint. Turning off result reuse and increasing concurrency does not reduce the amount scanned, so cost does not go down and may even go up. Because the SQL must be preserved and no new cluster is to be operated, reducing the amount scanned with Parquet conversion and partitioning is right.

prompt: A real-time multiplayer game company deploys game servers that communicate over UDP behind NLBs in Seoul and Frankfurt. Some customer firewalls need to manage fixed IPs in an allow list, and when one Region is unhealthy, players must be directed immediately to the healthy Region without a delay caused by DNS caching. It is good for players to enter the AWS backbone from the nearest edge. Game clients often connect with IP addresses registered in the allow list instead of domain names, and players are spread across Asia and Europe. When an entire Region stops responding, traffic must move to the healthy Region quickly, not in minutes. The server process uses a single UDP port, and the NLB supports UDP listeners. Some customers take a month to update an allow list, so the IPs must not change, and the company wants to reduce connection latency for players worldwide through the AWS backbone path. The client app is hard to modify for two months because of marketplace review. The Seoul and Frankfurt Regions use the same server image and the same UDP port. Waiting for the DNS record TTL to expire when one Region's NLB is unhealthy caused players to leave in the last outage. The operations team has 2 people. Which configuration MOST appropriately meets these requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create an AWS Global Accelerator standard accelerator, register the NLBs in both Regions as endpoint groups, and send traffic to the healthy Region with static anycast IPs and endpoint health checks.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Configure Amazon Route 53 latency routing records with health checks and lower the TTL to 60 seconds so that the record of an unhealthy Region is excluded from responses.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution, register the NLBs in both Regions as an origin group, and enable origin failover so that game UDP traffic also receives caching and acceleration at the edge.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Assign an Elastic IP address to the NLB in each Region and have customers allow both IPs, and change the client code so that the application retries with the other Region's IP on a connection failure. Keep a fixed IP in front of each Regional NLB so that the allow list does not change.

explanation: The correct answer is Global Accelerator. Two static anycast IPs satisfy the allow list requirement, endpoint health checks remove unhealthy endpoints immediately so that failover occurs without DNS cache delay, and traffic enters the AWS backbone at the nearest edge. It supports both TCP and UDP. Route 53 delays failover because of TTL and resolver caching and does not provide fixed IPs. CloudFront focuses on HTTP/HTTPS and WebSocket, so it does not suit UDP game traffic. The client retry approach requires client code changes and customer allow list management, which is a heavy operational burden. The requirements for fixed IPs, failover independent of DNS caching, and edge entry point to Global Accelerator, which provides anycast IPs.

prompt: A company set up an Amazon S3 bucket in ap-northeast-2 encrypted with SSE-KMS to be replicated cross-Region to a bucket in us-west-2 in a different AWS account. Versioning and a replication rule exist, but objects encrypted with AWS KMS are not replicated. Objects in the destination bucket must also be encrypted with a customer managed key in the destination account. The bucket already contains billions of objects, and newly written objects from now on are the replication targets. The destination account's security team wants to manage the key policy of the replica key directly. The replication targets are only new objects written from now on, and existing objects will be handled in a separate task. The source account's replication role has already been created, and ownership override is not needed. The destination account belongs to a separate organizational unit, and the destination key is a customer managed key created by that account. The replication latency target is within 15 minutes. The current replication rule applies to the whole bucket with no prefix filter, and the destination account already has a bucket policy that allows the replication role to write to the destination bucket. Replication status shows FAILED in the object metadata. Which two actions solve this problem and meet the requirements? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Specify an AWS managed key (aws/s3) as the replica encryption key of the destination bucket so that the destination account does not need to manage a key policy separately. AWS manages key rotation automatically, which reduces the security team's operational burden.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Replace the source key with a multi-Region key; S3 shares the key automatically through the multi-Region feature, so the replica key is not specified separately in the replication rule.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Grant the replication IAM role kms:Decrypt permission on the source key and kms:Encrypt permission on the destination key, and have the destination account's key policy allow use by the account that owns the source bucket (the replication role).

choices.label: D
choices.text: Grant the replication IAM role only s3:GetObjectVersion permission on the source object versions, which is enough to replicate even KMS-encrypted objects.

choices.label: E
choices.text: In the replication rule, explicitly enable replication of KMS-encrypted objects (SseKmsEncryptedObjects) and specify a customer managed key in the same Region as the destination bucket (us-west-2) as the replica encryption key.

explanation: The correct answers are enabling KMS object replication in the replication rule and specifying the destination key, together with granting permissions in the role and key policy. By default S3 does not replicate SSE-KMS objects, so you must turn on SseKmsEncryptedObjects and specify a key in the destination Region, the replication role needs permission to decrypt with the source key and encrypt with the destination key, and for cross-account, the key policy must allow it. AWS managed keys cannot be used cross-account, so they cannot be used. Even with a multi-Region key, S3 treats it like a single-Region key, so specifying the replica key is still required. GetObjectVersion alone cannot replicate KMS objects. The conditions that the destination account manages the key policy and a key in the destination Region must be used require both the KMS settings in the replication rule and the role permissions.

prompt: A game company's Amazon DynamoDB table receives concentrated reads on a few popular item keys during events, and the company has significantly overprovisioned read capacity. Most reads are fine with eventual consistency, responses at the microsecond level would be ideal, and the application calls the DynamoDB API with the Java SDK. Read requests are concentrated on a few keys, writes are relatively rare, and the development team must finish the improvement within 2 weeks before the next event. The table has about 200 million items with an average item size of 2 KB. Popular item keys are read tens of thousands of times per second during events but modified only dozens of times per day. Currently, read capacity is provisioned large to match the peak, and the application already uses only DynamoDB Query and GetItem calls. The team evaluated the number of cluster nodes and the maintenance cost, and DynamoDB read capacity cost accounts for half of the monthly cost. After an event ends, access frequency drops sharply, and eventual consistency is sufficient for read consistency. There are 2 operations staff. Which method MOST appropriately reduces both read cost and latency while minimizing code changes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create an Amazon ElastiCache cluster and implement cache lookup, update, and invalidation logic in the application code yourself so that reads are served from the cache.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Convert the table to a global table to spread reads across replicas in multiple Regions and have clients read from the replica in the nearest Region.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Place a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster in front of the table, replace the DynamoDB client with the DAX client by changing only the endpoint, and cache the reads.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Change the table to on-demand mode and use strongly consistent reads by default so that the most recent data is read.

explanation: DAX is a managed in-memory cache compatible with the DynamoDB API; it reduces eventually consistent reads to microseconds, absorbs repeated reads of frequently read keys to reduce the overprovisioning of read capacity, and requires only a code change at the level of replacing the client. ElastiCache requires you to write cache consistency and invalidation code yourself, which violates the requirement to minimize code changes. Global tables are for cross-Region replication and do not resolve read cost for hot keys or microsecond latency. Strongly consistent reads consume double the capacity and have no caching benefit, and are also the opposite direction from the requested latency reduction. Minimal code changes, microsecond responses, and tolerance of eventual consistency point to DAX, and global tables do not solve the read latency problem.

prompt: A company is migrating a 6 TB Windows file server to AWS. It wants to keep the on-premises Active Directory users and NTFS ACLs as they are and not change the existing share paths. File service must continue even if one Availability Zone fails, and the company wants to reduce operational burden such as server patching and storage management. The on-premises AD domain continues to operate on premises and is connected to AWS with AWS Direct Connect. 120 users use files all day, so the cutover is allowed only over a weekend. The file server has 40 shared folders, and NTFS permissions are set differently for each folder. Users connect from multiple branches, and a write freeze of a few hours over the weekend is acceptable for synchronizing the last changes before the cutover. The file server name can be pointed at the new server with a DNS alias. User accounts are in the on-premises AD domain, and the AWS file service must also be accessible with the same domain accounts. Users should not have to change their drive mappings after the migration, and one backup per day using a service feature is sufficient. Two Availability Zones in the Seoul Region are used. Which migration configuration is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Configure the file server yourself on two EC2 Windows instances with attached EBS volumes, make it redundant with DFS replication, and operate instance patching and backups yourself. Point the existing file server name at the new server with DNS to reduce path changes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create an Amazon EFS file system, copy the files with AWS DataSync, have Windows clients mount it with the NFS client feature, and map NTFS ACLs to POSIX permissions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Move the files to Amazon S3, have users access them with an S3 browser tool, control folder-level access with IAM policies, and replace the existing share names with bucket names.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Create Amazon FSx for Windows File Server in a Multi-AZ configuration, integrate it with Active Directory, copy the SMB files and NTFS permissions with AWS DataSync, and keep the existing share names with a DNS alias.

explanation: The correct answer is Multi-AZ FSx for Windows File Server. It is a fully managed Windows share that provides SMB, NTFS ACLs, and AD integration, withstands Availability Zone failures with Multi-AZ, keeps existing paths through a DNS alias, and DataSync copies ACLs and metadata while preserving them. An EC2 file server requires you to operate patching and DFS replication yourself, which conflicts with the operational burden requirement. EFS supports only NFS, so it cannot preserve NTFS ACLs and SMB paths. The S3 and IAM approach discards the existing AD permissions and share names. The conditions of NTFS ACLs, AD integration, Availability Zone failure tolerance, and reduced operational burden converge on Multi-AZ FSx for Windows.

prompt: A manufacturer needs to move 180 virtual servers on VMware and 20 non-virtualized physical servers to AWS. The data center contract ends in 4 months and application code cannot be modified. Services must keep operating during the migration, and cutover downtime per server must be within tens of minutes. The servers are a mix of Windows Server 2012 R2 (an OS that is out of Microsoft support but is on the MGN supported list, with .NET Framework 4.5 or later installed) and RHEL 7, and some are database servers with many changes, so replication lag must be monitored. The migration team prefers bulk work by wave because there are many servers. The migration must be completed before the data center contract ends, and waves are divided by application, taking dependencies between servers into account. A 1 Gbps Direct Connect already exists, and a bandwidth limit is needed so that replication traffic does not disrupt business. After the migration, the servers keep the same OS on Amazon EC2. Before each server's cutover, the team must be able to confirm the final sync and roll back to the source if there is a problem, and wants to run test cutovers repeatedly without interrupting operations. Administrator privileges to install agents have been obtained on all servers. Which method is MOST appropriate when grouping servers by application and migrating them in sequence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Export the VMware virtual servers as OVA files, upload them to Amazon S3, and create AMIs with VM Import/Export, and for physical servers take images and import them the same way. Run the image import jobs in parallel per server and validate the resulting AMIs.

choices.label: B
choices.text: First carry out a refactoring project that redesigns the applications with containers and serverless, and then switch services to the new architecture within 4 months.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Install the AWS Replication Agent on each server and perform continuous block-level replication with AWS Transform MGN (formerly AWS Application Migration Service); for each application and wave, validate with test instances and then launch the cutover instances.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Shut down all servers, take snapshots, move them to EC2 using an AWS Snow family device, and leave the service stopped during the migration period.

explanation: The correct answer is rehosting with continuous block-level replication in AWS Transform MGN (formerly Application Migration Service). The agent continuously replicates changed blocks regardless of whether servers are physical, virtual, or on another cloud, so migration proceeds while keeping the service running, validation is done with test instances before cutover, and bulk work by wave fits the 4-month schedule. Both OSs are on the MGN supported OS list (Windows Server 2012 R2 is an out-of-support OS, so an upgrade is recommended, and .NET Framework 4.5 or later is required). No code changes are needed, which also matches the constraints. Image export is a one-time copy that cannot sync changes, so downtime grows long, and it cannot be used for physical servers. Refactoring conflicts with the no-code-modification constraint and the 4-month schedule. Moving with a device while stopping the service violates the requirement to keep operating during the migration. The conditions of no code changes, cutover within tens of minutes, and wave-based work point to continuous block replication.

prompt: An insurance company's 40 AWS Lambda and Amazon ECS services keep the RDS MySQL password in plaintext in environment variables and change it manually once a year. A security audit required automatic rotation within 90 days and an access audit trail. Rotation must not interrupt the services and must not require redeploying applications. All the services use the AWS SDK, and there is no plan to upgrade the database engine. The audit team requires a record of who retrieved the credentials and when. The database and the secret must not get out of sync during password rotation, and existing connections must not be dropped during rotation. There are 40 services and a development team of 5, so code changes are limited to one or two lines of SDK calls. The audit team wants to check retrieval history in AWS CloudTrail. The service and time at which credentials were retrieved must remain in the audit log, and the company wants existing connections not to drop while connections switch to the new credentials after rotation. All services are in the Seoul Region and there is only one password per database. Which method meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Store the password in an AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store standard parameter, have an owner edit the value manually every quarter and then update the application settings, and record the time of the change in a change management ticket.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Store the credentials in AWS Secrets Manager, configure automatic rotation for RDS with the alternating users strategy on a 90-day schedule, and change the applications to retrieve the secret at runtime (including caching).

choices.label: C
choices.text: Put a KMS-encrypted password value in the environment variables, and have the deployment pipeline redeploy the services with the new value every 90 days.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increase the number of database users per service to reduce account sharing, and set an expiration date with the database password policy.

explanation: Secrets Manager supports automatic rotation for RDS, lets you set the rotation schedule, and allows access to be tracked with CloudTrail. The alternating users strategy rotates between two users, so the previous credentials remain valid until the next rotation, which matches the requirement of no service interruption during rotation, and if the application retrieves the secret at runtime instead of through an environment variable, it receives the rotated value without redeployment. Manual edits in Parameter Store violate the automatic rotation requirement. Keeping an encrypted value in an environment variable and redeploying periodically conflicts with the requirement to rotate without redeployment and without service interruption. Adding users and setting an expiration date would block services when passwords expire and also does not provide automatic rotation or an audit trail. Because the company must rotate automatically every 90 days without redeployment and keep retrieval history, the Secrets Manager alternating users strategy is right.

prompt: A media company serves video segments worldwide through Amazon CloudFront, and the origin is an on-premises packager in Seoul with limited bandwidth. Viewers are spread across several continents, and because each Regional edge cache requests the same object from the origin separately, the origin bandwidth saturates right after popular content is released. Requests for popular content concentrate in the 10 minutes after release, after which the cache hit ratio becomes high, and there is no budget this quarter for migrating the origin or adding bandwidth. The origin packager sits in a single data center in Seoul with a 1 Gbps uplink. The current cache hit ratio itself is not bad, but right after release, many edge caches request the same segment almost simultaneously, causing origin requests to surge. The application on the origin side cannot be modified, and only CloudFront settings can be changed. For popular content, origin requests rise to as much as 30 times normal in the 10 minutes after release, and afterward most are served from the cache. The cache TTL is already set appropriately per segment, so the TTL policy is not part of this improvement. Which method MOST effectively reduces the number of requests to the origin without expanding the origin?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Change the cache policy TTL to 0 so that every request fetches the latest object from the origin, align cache consistency with origin response headers, and also adjust origin-side cache control headers separately.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enable Origin Shield for that origin and choose the Origin Shield Region with the lowest latency to the origin (Seoul) so that requests from all cache layers pass through it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Add an NLB in front of the origin to distribute origin connections and have the load balancer absorb the number of connections coming from the edge.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Split the distribution by continent so that each distribution calls the origin directly, and use a separate cache key for each continent.

explanation: Origin Shield adds an additional caching layer between the Regional edge caches and the origin, collapsing requests for the same object into one so that they reach the origin almost only once; an on-premises origin with limited bandwidth is a typical use case, and you choose the Region with the lowest latency to the origin. Setting the TTL to 0 removes caching and actually causes origin requests to surge. An NLB only distributes connections and does not reduce duplicate requests for the same object nor solve the bandwidth limit. Splitting the distribution by continent separates the cache layers and increases duplicate requests. Because the company must reduce the number of origin requests without expanding the origin, Origin Shield, which places a single intermediate cache in front of the cache layers, is right.
